state.case_summary:
A 34-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 2-month history of progressively worsening morning headaches associated with nausea and vomiting, which did not fully resolve with analgesics. He later noted numbness, tingling, and weakness in both upper extremities, and intermittently experienced blurred or double vision, vertigo, and a clumsy gait. On neurologic examination, he had both vertical and horizontal nystagmus and gait ataxia; cranial nerve function was otherwise normal.

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a mildly hypodense, 30 × 40 × 40 mm mass lesion centered in the fourth ventricle region of the posterior fossa, without contrast enhancement or calcifications, and with surrounding brain edema and obstructive hydrocephalus. T2-weighted brain MRI confirmed a well-demarcated, relatively homogeneous mass filling the fourth ventricle, causing effacement of the fourth-ventricle outlets, cerebellar compression, and tonsillar herniation.
